best-broadway-shows.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows: March 2026

As Broadway enters the spring of 2026, the theater district offers an impressive blend of modern masterpieces and beloved revivals that collectively demonstrate the art form's remarkable range. This month's top-rated productions span from hip-hop infused historical drama to robot romance, absurdist political farce to timeless Disney spectacle.

**Hamilton** continues its reign as Broadway's highest-rated show, with critics maintaining that Lin-Manuel Miranda's revolutionary musical remains as vital and groundbreaking as ever. The production's fusion of hip-hop storytelling with American history earns a 90/100 score across 42 reviews, cementing its status as an essential theatrical experience.

Close behind, **Maybe Happy Ending** distinguishes itself as one of the season's most original offerings, with its unconventional robot love story earning an 85/100 rating and widespread praise for emotional depth that transcends its quirky premise. Meanwhile, **Oh, Mary!** proves that irreverent comedy has a firm place among Broadway's elite, with Cole Escola's absurdist take on Mary Todd Lincoln delighting critics and earning an 84/100 score.

The current lineup also showcases Broadway's enduring classics, with **The Book of Mormon** and **The Lion King** both maintaining 83/100 ratings, while **Chicago** and **Hadestown** demonstrate that both stripped-down and elaborately staged productions can achieve critical acclaim. Daniel Radcliffe's intimate **Every Brilliant Thing** offers a counterpoint to the spectacle of **Harry Potter and the Cursed Child**, proving that Broadway's appeal spans from one-person shows to technical extravaganzas.

With an average critic score of 84/100 across all featured productions, March 2026 presents an exceptionally strong moment to experience Broadway at its most diverse and accomplished.

best-broadway-shows-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that opened in 2020 represent a fascinating snapshot of a season cut dramatically short. Before the pandemic shuttered theaters that March, a handful of productions managed to make their mark, and several have proven their staying power in the years since.

Leading our rankings is **Les Misérables**, which scores 83/100 across 9 reviews for its grittier reboot at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre. This reimagined production has won over most critics with its fresh approach to the beloved musical, though it hasn't achieved universal acclaim.

**A Soldier's Play** stands out as perhaps the season's most significant dramatic achievement, earning 78/100 from 29 reviews. Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning work finally received its long-overdue Broadway debut in a revival that critics consistently praise for its powerful examination of race and justice in America—themes that have only grown more resonant in the years since its opening.

The season also brought **Grand Horizons**, a more modest but well-crafted boulevard comedy featuring acclaimed performances from Jane Alexander and James Cromwell (73/100), and Laura Linney's solo turn in **My Name is Lucy Barton** (71/100), an adaptation that showcases the actress's considerable talents even as critics remain split on the theatrical adaptation itself.

Rounding out our list is Ivo van Hove's polarizing **West Side Story** reimagining (68/100), which continues to spark debate about how radically classic works can—or should—be reinterpreted for contemporary audiences.

Whether you're seeking powerful drama, innovative reimaginings, or intimate character studies, these surviving productions from 2020's abbreviated season offer compelling options for your next theater outing.

Leading the pack is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama that continues to mesmerize audiences with Deirdre O'Connell's extraordinary lip-sync performance to real interview recordings. Critics describe it as unlike anything else on Broadway—a bold artistic statement that pushes theatrical boundaries.

**The Phantom of the Opera**, Andrew Lloyd Webber's legendary mega-musical, proves that spectacle and infectious melodies never go out of style, even as it approaches its historic run's conclusion. Meanwhile, **Pass Over**, Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's urgent drama blending Beckett with the Exodus story, earned its place as Broadway's first show back, setting a powerful tone for the industry's reopening.

The 2021 class also includes virtuosic solo performances like **Lackawanna Blues**, epic theatrical achievements such as **The Lehman Trilogy**, and bold reimaginings like the gender-swapped **Company** revival. From the immersive **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club** to the pop-infused energy of **SIX**, these productions showcase remarkable range and artistic ambition.

Whether you're catching these shows during their final months or discovering them for the first time, this guide highlights the productions that helped Broadway roar back to life.

best-broadway-shows-2022.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows from 2022

As we look back from March 2026, the class of 2022 stands out as a remarkable year for Broadway, marked by an exceptional concentration of Pulitzer Prize-winning works and critically acclaimed revivals that continue to resonate with audiences.

Leading the pack is **Kimberly Akimbo**, the quirky musical about a teenager with a rare aging condition that critics have embraced as a near-perfect achievement. David Lindsay-Abaire and Jeanine Tesori's collaboration earns widespread praise for its delicate balance of humor and heartbreak, proving that small-scale stories can deliver the biggest emotional impact.

The year also represents a fitting tribute to Stephen Sondheim, who passed away in late 2021. **Into the Woods** arrives as a stripped-down revival that critics celebrate as both a worthy memorial and a vital reinterpretation, demonstrating the enduring power of the legendary composer's work.

**A Strange Loop**, Michael R. Jackson's meta-musical about a Black gay writer creating a musical about a Black gay writer, brings a brazenly original voice to Broadway. The Pulitzer winner's unflinching honesty and structural audacity earn critical acclaim as a groundbreaking achievement in American musical theater.

Beyond these standouts, 2022 proves to be a banner year for serious drama, with four Pulitzer Prize-winning plays reaching Broadway: Suzan-Lori Parks' **Topdog/Underdog**, Tom Stoppard's **Leopoldstadt**, Stephen Adly Guirgis's **Between Riverside and Crazy**, Paula Vogel's **How I Learned to Drive**, and Martyna Majok's **Cost of Living**. This unprecedented concentration of award-winning work reflects Broadway's commitment to substantive storytelling.

With an average critic score of 83/100 across these ten productions, the 2022 season offers theatergoers a wealth of exceptional choices that continue to define contemporary American theater.

Close behind, "The Phantom of the Opera" proves that Andrew Lloyd Webber's mega-musical remains a spectacular theatrical experience, even if some critics find it campy by contemporary standards.

Meanwhile, ambitious epics like "The Lehman Trilogy" demonstrate Broadway's capacity for sweeping theatrical storytelling, while revivals including the gender-swapped "Company" and the immersive "Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club" prove that reimagined classics can feel vital and urgent.

From Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's "Pass Over"—which appropriately served as Broadway's post-shutdown reopening—to the pop-infused energy of "SIX" and Lynn Nottage's warm-hearted "Clyde's," these productions capture a transformative moment in American theater. Whether you're discovering these shows for the first time or revisiting old favorites, this guide offers a comprehensive look at the plays that helped Broadway find its voice again.

The diversity of voices and stories—from Jordan E. Cooper's provocative satire **Ain't No Mo'** to Mike Birbiglia's intimate solo show—illustrates a season that prioritized both artistic ambition and varied perspectives. Close behind is **Stranger Things: The First Shadow**, a West End transfer that proved theatrical adaptations of popular IP could achieve genuine artistic merit through technical innovation and strong storytelling rather than mere fan service.

Solo performances made their mark as well, with Alex Edelman's **Just for Us** and Jodie Comer's **Prima Facie** demonstrating the continued vitality of one-person shows. Meanwhile, James Ijames's Pulitzer Prize-winning **Fat Ham** brought fresh perspective to classic literature through its Hamlet adaptation set at a Black family barbecue.

Whether you're catching final performances of these productions or exploring recordings and regional productions, these ten plays represent some of the finest theatrical work to emerge from recent Broadway seasons.
